summary: Understand how money works: earn, spend, save, give, and protect yourself from financial traps.
goals: Tell needs from wants and plan a simple monthly budget
Explain how saving, interest and inflation affect the value of money over time
Spot common money traps such as pyramid schemes and get-rich-quick offers
idea: Money is a tool, not a goal. Financial literacy means understanding how to earn it, spend it wisely, save for the future, give generously and avoid traps. Habits formed as a teenager, such as saving something from every income, often last a lifetime.

Two ideas surprise most people. Compound interest means your savings earn money on the money they have already earned, so starting early matters more than starting big. Inflation means prices rise over time, so money kept idle loses buying power. Offers that promise huge returns with no risk are almost always scams.
oneLine: Pay yourself first, plan before you spend, let time work for you and avoid anything that promises easy riches.
steps: Earn: list every source of income, such as allowance, gifts, small jobs or a business
Spend: sort spending into needs and wants; plan with a simple rule, for example 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and giving, adjusted to your situation
Save: pay yourself first by moving savings out as soon as money arrives; set a clear target, such as an emergency fund
Give and protect: set aside something to share; check any investment offer: who regulates it, can I withdraw, and does it promise guaranteed high returns?
scenarioSetup: Femi earns 10,000 naira a month from tutoring younger children. A friend says, 'Put it in this online scheme: double your money in 2 weeks, guaranteed!'
scenarioWrong: Femi invests 10,000 naira. After one week, the platform disappears and the money is gone.
scenarioBetter: Earn: 10,000 naira monthly
Spend: 5,000 on needs (transport, data), 3,000 on wants, 2,000 saved and given
Save: transfer 1,000 naira to a savings account on payday and 1,000 for an emergency fund
Protect: he checks the scheme, finds no regulation and a guaranteed double, which is a classic scam warning, and refuses.
mistakes: Mistake: spending first and saving what is left. Fix: Pay yourself first.
Mistake: borrowing for wants. Fix: Wait and save, or find a cheaper option.
Mistake: believing 'guaranteed' high returns. Fix: Higher return means higher risk; guaranteed riches are a red flag.
lab: (5 min) List your income and your top five regular expenses
(10 min) Draw a simple monthly budget with needs, wants and saving
(10 min) Calculate how 2,000 naira saved monthly grows over a year (with and without interest) and discuss
(5 min) Spot the red flags in three sample investment ads
reflect: What does money mean to me, and what messages did I learn at home?
Which spending is a want pretending to be a need?
What am I saving for, and by when?
takeaways: Time and compounding help early savers
Guaranteed fast riches are a scam warning
challenge: Track every naira you earn and spend for one week, then create a monthly budget and a savings target with a date. Share the plan with an adult for advice and add your budget to your portfolio.

check.q: What does 'pay yourself first' mean?
o: Move savings out as soon as you receive money

check.q: Why does starting to save early matter?
o: Because compound interest grows over time

check.q: An offer promises to double your money in two weeks with no risk. What should you conclude?
o: It is very likely a scam
It is guaranteed by the government
It is a normal bank product

summary: Turn a real problem into a simple business idea and test it with real customers.
goals: Describe a customer problem, a solution, a price and a way to reach customers
Calculate simple profit: revenue minus costs
Run a low-cost test of the idea with at least five potential customers
idea: Entrepreneurship means spotting a problem and creating value for people, often for money, sometimes for social good. Many successful businesses started as small experiments by people who noticed a real need. You do not need a big idea or lots of money; you need a customer who cares enough to pay or use it.

The biggest mistake new entrepreneurs make is building too much before asking anyone. The lean approach is: talk to customers, build the smallest version that could work, test it, and improve. A business that cannot cover its costs is a hobby, so understanding revenue, costs and profit is essential.
oneLine: Start with a real problem, test the smallest version with real customers and watch your costs.
steps: Problem: describe one real problem and who has it, for example 'Students in my area struggle to print assignments'
Customer and solution: say exactly who will buy, what you will offer and why it is better than the alternative
Numbers: set a price and work out costs, then profit = revenue minus costs
Test: sell or demonstrate to five people before spending big; ask for honest feedback and adjust
scenarioSetup: Gbenga notices that his neighbours in a block of flats wait a long time for a fruit seller who comes only on Saturdays. He imagines a grand fruit app.
scenarioWrong: He spends two months and a lot of money building an app before asking neighbours, then finds that they prefer ordering on WhatsApp.
scenarioBetter: Problem: neighbours want fresh fruit on weekdays
Customer and solution: weekly fruit boxes delivered by him and a friend, ordered by WhatsApp
Numbers: box sells at 3,000 naira, costs 2,000, profit 1,000 per box
Test: he offers five boxes this week, collects feedback, then adjusts the price and the box size.
mistakes: Mistake: ignoring costs. Fix: Count everything, including your time.
Mistake: loving your idea more than customers' needs. Fix: Ask customers and listen.
Mistake: waiting for perfect. Fix: Test the smallest version quickly.
lab: (5 min) List three problems you see around you
(10 min) Pick one and complete Problem, Customer, Solution, numbers
(10 min) Plan a five-person test and a simple script of questions
(5 min) Pitch your idea in 60 seconds
reflect: Which problem do I care about enough to work on?
Who would be my first five customers?
What am I afraid of in starting a business?
challenge: Test your idea with at least five real people this week (a free sample, a mock-up or an order). Record what they said, what you will change and your costs and profit. Add the results to your portfolio.

check.q: What is the best first step in a new business idea?
o: Talk to potential customers about their problem

check.q: How do you calculate profit?
Why test with five people first?
o: To learn cheaply whether your idea is wanted

summary: Solve problems for real people using the five design thinking stages.
goals: Name the five design thinking stages: Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test
Interview a user and capture a clear 'how might we' question
Build a cheap prototype and improve it from feedback
idea: Design thinking is a human-centred way to solve problems, popularised by Stanford's d.school. Instead of starting with a solution, you start with people: you observe, ask and listen to understand what they really need, and then create and test options with them.

The stages are not a straight line; you may loop back as you learn. A prototype can be a drawing, a cardboard model or a role-play, anything that lets you test an idea cheaply. The aim is to fail early and cheaply so that you succeed later.
oneLine: Understand the person, define the problem, create many ideas, build quickly and test with real users.
steps: Empathise: observe and interview real users to learn what they do, think and feel
Define: write a 'how might we' question, such as 'How might we help junior students find the library quickly?'
Ideate: generate many ideas, then choose one or two to try
Prototype and Test: build a rough version, put it in front of users, watch, listen and improve
scenarioSetup: A group of students wants to reduce queues at the school canteen. They quickly decide to buy a card-payment machine.
scenarioWrong: After spending the money, they find the queues are caused by the canteen layout, not the payment method.
scenarioBetter: Empathise: they watch the queue for three days and interview students and staff
Define: 'How might we help students order and collect food faster in the 20-minute break?'
Ideate: pre-order slips, a two-lane system, a pickup shelf
Prototype and Test: they try pre-order slips with one class for a week, measure time saved and adjust.
mistakes: Mistake: designing for yourself. Fix: Talk to the real users.
Mistake: falling in love with the first idea. Fix: Make several prototypes.
Mistake: building complete products before testing. Fix: Use paper and cardboard first.
lab: (5 min) Pick a user (a classmate, parent or teacher) and a small problem in their day
(10 min) Interview them with five open questions
(10 min) Write a 'how might we' question and sketch three ideas
(5 min) Create a simple paper prototype and test it with another group
reflect: Whose problem would I like to understand better?
What assumption did I make that the user corrected?
What is the cheapest way to test my idea?
challenge: Take one real problem through all five stages with at least two real users and record each stage with photos or notes. Add the process and your final prototype to your portfolio; it can become part of your capstone.

check.q: What is the first stage of design thinking?
A 'how might we' question helps you:
o: Frame a problem as an opportunity to explore

check.q: Why make a cheap prototype?
o: To learn quickly and cheaply from user feedback

summary: Explore careers by matching interests, strengths, values and the real world of work.
goals: Use interests, skills, values and the job market to shortlist three careers
Learn how to research a career using at least three sources
Prepare questions for an informational interview with a professional
idea: Choosing a career is not one big decision made at 17; it is a series of experiments. The best way to decide is to gather information: what do people actually do all day, what skills and education are needed, what does it pay, and how might the job change because of technology?

Think in four circles: what you enjoy (interests), what you are good at (skills), what matters to you (values) and what the world needs and pays for (market). Where they overlap is a good place to explore. An informational interview, a short conversation with someone doing the job, is one of the best research tools you have.
oneLine: Explore, don't guess: match yourself to the world of work and talk to people doing the job.
steps: Interests and Skills: list what you enjoy and do well, using your Strengths Triangle from Week 3
Values: list what matters most to you in work, such as helping people, creativity, security or income
Market: research three careers: tasks, training, pay, demand and future trends from at least three sources
Test: arrange an informational interview, a job shadow or a small project to try the work
scenarioSetup: Samuel says he wants to be a doctor because his uncle is one and everyone says it is prestigious. He has never watched a doctor work or talked to one about the training.
scenarioWrong: He enters a science stream, struggles in Biology and feels trapped because he never explored alternatives.
scenarioBetter: Interests and Skills: he enjoys helping people and is good at explaining and solving puzzles
Values: meaningful work and steady income
Market: he researches medicine, physiotherapy and health technology, learning about training length and demand
Test: he interviews a physiotherapist and spends a day at a clinic, then adjusts his subjects.
mistakes: Mistake: choosing only for prestige or pay. Fix: Match values and strengths.
Mistake: relying on one source. Fix: Use at least three, including a person in the job.
Mistake: thinking the decision is final. Fix: Treat it as an experiment you can adjust.
lab: (5 min) Write your top three interests, skills and values
(10 min) Shortlist three careers and research one using at least three sources
(10 min) Prepare five questions for an informational interview
(5 min) Role-play the first two minutes of an interview
reflect: What career messages have I received from family and friends?
What work would I do even if no one noticed?
What skills would I need to build now for my shortlisted careers?
takeaways: Explore several careers through research and conversations
Match interests, skills, values and market
Informational interviews are powerful and free
challenge: Complete a Career Exploration Sheet for three careers and carry out one informational interview (in person, by phone or message). Write a short summary of what you learned and add both to your portfolio.

check.q: What is an informational interview?
o: A short conversation with someone in a career to learn about it

check.q: Why research a career in at least three sources?
o: To get a balanced and accurate picture

check.q: Which approach is best for career choice?

summary: Write a clear, honest CV and personal statement that show your impact, not just your duties.
goals: Structure a one-page CV with contact details, profile, education, experience and skills
Write achievement bullets using Action verb + What + Result
Write a personal statement that tells your story and links to a goal
idea: A CV (curriculum vitae) is a short summary of who you are and what you can do. Employers or admissions officers often read it for under a minute, so clarity and relevance matter more than length. A personal statement adds the story behind the facts: why you want this opportunity and what makes you suited to it.

The strongest CVs show impact, not duties. 'Responsible for the school club' tells little; 'Led a 12-member debate club and increased attendance from 5 to 20 members in one term' shows a result. As a young person, you can include school projects, volunteering, leadership roles, sports, languages and digital skills.
oneLine: Show impact with action verbs and numbers, keep it to one page, and tailor it to the opportunity.
steps: Collect: list your experiences: projects, clubs, jobs, volunteering and awards
Write bullets: begin with an action verb, say what you did and add the result or number: 'Organised a book drive that collected 150 books for a local library'
Structure: contact details, a two-line profile, education, experience and activities, skills, references on request, all on one page with clean formatting
Tailor and proofread: adjust for each opportunity and have someone check spelling and facts
scenarioSetup: Amaka applies for a youth internship. Her CV says, 'I am hardworking and responsible' and lists 'Member of school choir' with no details.
scenarioWrong: The recruiter sees no evidence and moves on to a more specific CV.
scenarioBetter: Profile: 'Year 11 student with a passion for community education and strong organising skills'

Bullets: 'Organised a weekend reading club for 15 primary pupils for six months'; 'Raised 25,000 naira for school supplies through a bake sale'; 'Sang in the school choir and led warm-ups for 30 members'
Skills: Microsoft Word, public speaking, Igbo and English
She asks her teacher to proofread and tailors it to the internship's focus on education.
mistakes: Mistake: lists of duties with no results. Fix: Add numbers and outcomes.
Mistake: spelling errors and inconsistent formatting. Fix: Proofread twice and ask a friend.
Mistake: unprofessional email addresses. Fix: Use a simple name-based email.
lab: (5 min) List five experiences and one result for each
(10 min) Write three achievement bullets using Action + What + Result
(10 min) Draft a 100-word personal statement
(5 min) Swap with a partner for a proofread and one improvement
reflect: What have I achieved that I forget to mention?
What story do I want my personal statement to tell?
Whom can I ask for a reference?
challenge: Create your one-page CV and a 150-word personal statement, ask a teacher or mentor for feedback, and revise. Add the final versions to your portfolio, ready to use for opportunities.

check.q: Which bullet is strongest?
o: Led a 12-member debate club and grew attendance from 5 to 20 in one term

check.q: How long should a CV for a young person be?
What does a personal statement add to a CV?
o: The story and motivation behind the facts

summary: Prepare for and perform well in interviews using research, STAR stories and good questions.
goals: Research an organisation and role before an interview
Answer behavioural questions using the STAR method: Situation, Task, Action, Result
Ask two thoughtful questions at the end and close the interview well
idea: An interview is a conversation where both sides check whether there is a good fit. Interviewers want to know three things: can you do the job, will you do it, and will you fit in? You answer these by showing preparation, giving specific examples and being honest and positive.

Most interviews include behavioural questions such as 'Tell me about a time you worked in a team'. The STAR method gives a simple structure: describe the Situation, the Task, the Action you took and the Result. Preparing three or four STAR stories in advance means you can adapt them to almost any question.
oneLine: Research, prepare three STAR stories, ask good questions and show your personality.
steps: Situation: set the scene briefly, 'In Year 10, my group had to organise a charity bake sale.'
Task: explain your responsibility, 'I was asked to manage the budget.'
Action: describe what you did, step by step, using 'I', 'I made a list of costs, set prices and tracked sales daily.'
Result: share the outcome and the lesson: 'We raised 40,000 naira, 20 per cent above our target, and I learned to track numbers early.'
scenarioSetup: Dami is interviewed for a volunteer role at a children's hospital. The panel asks, 'Tell us about a time you solved a problem.'
scenarioWrong: Dami says, 'I am good at solving problems, I always try my best,' and gives no example. The panel is not convinced.
scenarioBetter: Situation: 'When my class library had too few books...'
Task: 'I wanted to build a collection of 100 books in a term.'
Action: 'I asked neighbours to donate, set up a collection box at the church and posted a list on WhatsApp.'
Result: 'We collected 130 books, and I learned that asking directly works.' He then asks, 'How do volunteers get supported in their first month?'
mistakes: Mistake: vague answers without examples. Fix: Use STAR stories.
Mistake: arriving unprepared about the organisation. Fix: Research its mission, values and recent news.
Mistake: no questions at the end. Fix: Prepare two questions.
lab: (5 min) Choose three experiences and outline each in STAR form
(10 min) Practise answering common questions in pairs; the interviewer notes strengths
(10 min) Practise your first impression: greeting, handshake or smile, and a 30-second 'tell me about yourself'
(5 min) Swap roles and compare feedback
reflect: What are my three best stories and what do they show?
How do I feel before interviews, and what helps?
What questions would help me learn about an organisation?
challenge: Complete a mock interview with a teacher, parent or mentor, using at least two STAR stories and two questions. Ask for feedback and write down three improvements. Send a thank-you message afterwards and add your notes to your portfolio.

check.q: In STAR, what does the 'R' stand for?
Why research the organisation before an interview?
o: To show interest and tailor your answers

check.q: At the end of an interview, you should:
o: Ask one or two thoughtful questions

summary: Show professionalism in your emails, meetings, messages, dress and behaviour.
goals: Write a clear professional email with a subject line, greeting, message and sign-off
Apply basic meeting etiquette: punctuality, preparation and respect
Choose appropriate dress, tone and language for different settings
idea: Professional etiquette is a set of habits that show respect for other people's time and trust. They are simple but powerful: arriving on time, replying promptly, using polite language and being prepared. People often decide in the first few minutes whether you are reliable, and these habits are how they decide.

Digital settings need the same care. A message to a teacher or employer is not a message to a friend: it needs a clear subject, a greeting, full sentences and a thank-you. A chat message that says only 'Hi' forces the other person to wait and guess; a clear message saves time and shows maturity.
oneLine: Be on time, be prepared, be polite and be clear, in person and online.
steps: On time: arrive 10 minutes early; if delayed, message early and apologise
Prepared: know the agenda, bring what you need and have questions ready
Polite: greet people, use names and titles, thank them and listen without interrupting
Clear: in emails use a subject line, greeting, one purpose, specific request and sign-off; dress and speak appropriately for the setting
scenarioSetup: Chiamaka needs to ask a company for a work-experience placement. She sends a WhatsApp voice note at midnight saying, 'Hello, I want to come and work for you.'
scenarioWrong: She gets no reply because the message is unprofessional, unclear and sent at an odd hour.
scenarioBetter: Subject: Work experience request: Chiamaka Okafor, Year 11
Greeting and purpose: 'Dear Mr Bello, I am a Year 11 student at Greenfield School and I would like to ask about a two-week work-experience placement.'
Detail and request: 'I am interested in accounting and could attend from 3 to 14 June. May I send my CV?'
Close: 'Thank you for your time. Kind regards, Chiamaka.' She sends it during working hours.
mistakes: Mistake: using slang and emojis in formal messages. Fix: Match the tone to the audience.
Mistake: 'Hi' with no content. Fix: Say who you are and why you are writing.
Mistake: ignoring replies. Fix: Respond within 24 hours.
lab: (5 min) Rewrite a casual message into a professional email
(10 min) Role-play arriving at a meeting: introduction, handshake, small talk, agenda
(10 min) Practise a phone call to ask about an opportunity
(5 min) Discuss what to wear for three different settings
reflect: What first impression do I give in messages and in person?
Which etiquette habit would help me most right now?
Who models professionalism well, and what do they do?
takeaways: Be clear and respectful in every message
challenge: Send at least one real professional email or message (for example to a teacher, a company or a mentor) using the format learned. Record the response and what you would improve. Add the message to your portfolio.

check.q: What should a professional email always have?
o: A clear subject line, greeting, purpose and sign-off

check.q: If you will be late to a meeting, you should:
Why match your tone to your audience?
o: Formal settings need respect and clarity
It is a rule only in schools

summary: Plan and carry out a community project that creates measurable benefit.
goals: Identify a community need by listening to people affected
Plan a service project with goals, tasks and a way to measure impact
Share results and thank partners
idea: Community impact means creating positive, lasting change for others. The best service projects respond to a need the community has named, rather than a solution someone imagined. They also measure results: how many people were helped, what changed and what could be improved.

Service learning combines action with reflection: you do something useful and you think about what it taught you. It builds empathy, teamwork, project skills and civic responsibility, and it is increasingly valued by universities and employers.
oneLine: Listen first, plan carefully, act together, and measure what changed.
steps: Need: talk to people in your community and write the need in their words
Plan: set a goal, tasks, roles, budget and timeline; seek permission and partners such as a school, mosque, church or local leader
Act: carry out the project safely and respectfully, with adult supervision where needed
Measure and share: count the impact (people helped, items collected, hours), gather feedback, thank partners and share what you learned
scenarioSetup: A group of students notices that some children on their street walk to school in worn-out sandals.
scenarioWrong: They collect shoes without asking families and leave a box at the school gate. Many shoes are the wrong size and nobody knows who they are for.
scenarioBetter: Need: they talk to parents and the headteacher and learn the main need is shoes for 40 children aged 6 to 10
Plan: collect and clean donated shoes, measure sizes, deliver privately with the headteacher
Act: two weekends of collecting, one day of fitting
Measure: 38 of 40 children fitted; feedback from parents; thank-you notes sent to donors; photos shared with permission.
mistakes: Mistake: assuming you know what people need. Fix: Ask them.
Mistake: ignoring dignity and privacy. Fix: Serve respectfully and protect identities.
Mistake: forgetting to measure. Fix: Count and gather feedback.
lab: (5 min) List three needs people have told you about
(10 min) Plan a mini-project with goal, tasks, roles and measure
(10 min) Write a short invitation or request for help and role-play asking a local leader
(5 min) Decide how you will record and share impact
reflect: Which issues in my community matter most to me?
What did I learn from people I serve?
How can my project continue after I stop?
challenge: Carry out a small community project with at least two other people. Record your hours, your impact numbers and photos or feedback (with permission). Add your Community Service record to your portfolio.

check.q: What is the best first step in a community project?
o: Listen to people to learn the real need

check.q: Why measure the impact of a project?
o: To know what changed and how to improve

check.q: What does service learning add to service?

summary: Find, approach and learn from a mentor, and pay it forward by mentoring someone younger.
goals: Describe what a mentor does and how a mentoring relationship works
Approach a potential mentor with a clear, polite request
Plan to mentor someone and share what you know
idea: A mentor is someone with more experience who offers guidance, feedback and encouragement. Mentors do not do the work for you; they help you see options, avoid mistakes and grow faster. Many successful people can name a mentor who changed their path.

Mentoring works best when the mentee takes the lead: prepares goals and questions, respects the mentor's time, acts on advice and says thank you. You can also be a mentor now: tutoring a younger student or sharing what you learned is mentoring and strengthens your own skills.
oneLine: Prepare, ask, act on advice and thank; then pass it on by mentoring someone else.
steps: Prepare: decide what you want help with (a goal), and look for people whose work you admire and who are reachable
Ask: send a short, specific request, 'Could I have 20 minutes of your time once a month for three months to learn about graphic design?'
Act: come with questions, take notes, try the advice and report back on what happened
Thank and give back: show gratitude, share your progress and look for someone younger you can help
scenarioSetup: Ibrahim wants to become a software developer. He sends a long message to a stranger asking, 'Please be my mentor, I need you to teach me everything.'
scenarioWrong: The stranger does not reply because the request is vague and heavy.
scenarioBetter: Prepare: he chooses a local developer whose talk he enjoyed and defines a goal: build his first website by December
Ask: 'Dear Mrs Okoro, I enjoyed your talk. Could I ask three questions about learning web development, over 20 minutes by phone?'
Act: he builds a small page after her advice and sends a screenshot with thanks
Thank and give back: after three months, she agrees to a monthly check-in and he starts a coding club for younger students.
mistakes: Mistake: expecting the mentor to do everything. Fix: You drive; they guide.
Mistake: not following up. Fix: Share progress; it keeps mentors engaged.
Mistake: waiting for a 'perfect' mentor. Fix: Seek several mentors for different areas.
lab: (5 min) Write one goal and the type of mentor who could help
(10 min) Draft a short message asking for a conversation
(10 min) Role-play a first mentoring conversation in pairs
(5 min) Plan how you could mentor a younger student
reflect: Who has already mentored me, formally or informally?
What am I afraid of when asking for help?
What could I teach someone younger?
takeaways: Mentors guide; you do the work
A specific, polite request gets better replies
challenge: Reach out to a potential mentor with a specific request, or begin mentoring a younger student for at least three sessions. Record what happened and what you learned and add it to your portfolio.

check.q: What does a mentor mainly do?
Which request is best?
o: Could I have 20 minutes to ask three questions about learning web development?

check.q: How can a young person also practise mentoring?
o: By tutoring or guiding a younger student
By waiting until they are old

summary: Turn a year of learning into one clear capstone plan with a problem, solution, timeline and proof of impact.
goals: Define a capstone problem, audience and goal in one paragraph
Create a week-by-week plan to the Summit with roles and milestones
Choose how you will prove your project worked
idea: Your capstone is where the whole year comes together: a real problem (critical thinking), a creative solution (design thinking), a plan (project management), clear delivery (communication) and measured results (community impact). A strong capstone is focused: it solves one problem well rather than trying to fix everything.

Many projects fail not because the idea is weak but because the plan is vague. Work backwards from the Summit date, list what must be done each week, assign owners and decide what evidence you will show, such as before and after data, testimonials, photos or user feedback.
oneLine: Choose one problem, plan backwards from the Summit and decide how you will prove your impact.
steps: Problem: write who has the problem, what it is and how you know
Solution: describe your idea and why it is better than what exists
Plan: list weekly milestones and owners from now to the Summit, with a backup for the biggest risk
Proof and pitch: decide what evidence you will gather and outline a five-minute pitch: story, problem, solution, results, next steps
scenarioSetup: Gift wants to do a capstone about 'improving education in Nigeria'. She has three months and no budget.
scenarioWrong: The topic is too big, she does not know where to start and ends up with a general presentation with no evidence.
scenarioBetter: Problem: 'Children in my street do not have help with homework after school.'
Solution: a free weekly homework club run by volunteer students
Plan: Week 48 recruit 5 volunteers and a venue; Week 49 run two sessions and collect feedback; Week 50 present results
Proof: attendance numbers, a short survey, a photo and a parent testimonial, with a pitch outline ready.
mistakes: Mistake: choosing a topic that is too broad. Fix: Narrow to a specific group and place.
Mistake: leaving evidence to the end. Fix: Collect proof as you go.
Mistake: working alone with no feedback. Fix: Show your plan to a mentor this week.
lab: (5 min) Write your problem statement
(10 min) Describe your solution in one sentence and one sketch
(10 min) Create a three-week plan with owners and a risk backup
(5 min) Pitch your plan to a partner in 60 seconds
reflect: Which skills from this year will my capstone rely on most?
What is the biggest risk to finishing on time, and what is my backup?
Who can mentor or advise my project?
takeaways: A focused problem makes a stronger capstone
Planning backwards from the date prevents last-minute panic
challenge: Finalise your capstone topic, team roles (if working in a team), week-by-week plan and evidence plan, and share it with a mentor for feedback. Add the plan to your portfolio.

check.q: What makes a capstone strong?
o: A focused problem, a clear plan and evidence of impact

check.q: Why plan backwards from the Summit date?
o: It shows what must be done each week to finish on time

check.q: What kind of evidence could prove a project worked?
o: Before and after data, feedback and photos

summary: Rehearse your capstone presentation, prepare for questions and fix the details that matter.
goals: Deliver your pitch within the time limit with confident delivery
Answer tough questions using a calm structure: Pause, Answer, Evidence
Run a tech and logistics check so nothing surprises you on the day
idea: Rehearsal turns knowledge into performance. Professional speakers rehearse many times, because the first run-through always reveals unclear slides, missing points or timing problems. Rehearsing out loud, standing up, with a timer, is very different from reading your slides silently.

Questions are not attacks; they are interest. Prepare by listing the ten hardest questions you could be asked and practising answers. When you do not know an answer, it is better to say, 'I do not know yet, but here is how I would find out,' than to guess. Finally, check the details: internet, slides, microphone, clothes, timing and a backup copy.
oneLine: Rehearse out loud, prepare for hard questions and check every detail before the big day.
methodName: Rehearse, Q and A, Tech Check
steps: Rehearse: run three full rehearsals: alone with a timer, in front of a friend, and in front of a small audience; adjust after each
Q and A: list ten likely questions; answer with Pause, Answer, Evidence: take a breath, give a direct answer and support it with a fact
Tech check: test your slides, internet, audio, camera, lighting and backup files; arrive early or log in 15 minutes before
Feedback: ask two people for one strength and one improvement and apply it
scenarioSetup: Daniel has a great project but has never rehearsed. At the practice session he runs out of time, loses his place and answers a question with 'I do not know.'
scenarioWrong: He decides he is 'bad at presenting' and plans to read from his slides at the Summit.
scenarioBetter: Rehearse: three runs, cutting two slides and fixing his timing to five minutes
Q and A: he writes ten likely questions, practises answers and prepares one for 'How will it last?'
Tech check: he saves a copy on his phone and tests the microphone
Result: at the next practice he finishes in 4:50 and answers a hard question calmly.
mistakes: Mistake: rehearsing silently in your head. Fix: Say it out loud, standing up.
Mistake: ignoring timing. Fix: Use a timer and cut content.
Mistake: leaving tech checks to the day. Fix: Test everything early.
lab: (5 min) Run your pitch alone with a timer
(10 min) Present to a small group and collect feedback
(10 min) Practise answering five tough questions with Pause, Answer, Evidence
(5 min) Complete a checklist: slides, backup, device, outfit, arrival time
reflect: Which part of my presentation feels weakest?
What is the hardest question I could be asked, and what is my honest answer?
What will I do to feel calm on the day?
takeaways: Rehearsal reveals what you cannot see alone
Questions are interest, so prepare for them
challenge: Do three full rehearsals of your capstone presentation (alone, with a friend, with a small group) and record the timing and feedback each time. Add your rehearsal log and improved slides to your portfolio.

check.q: Why rehearse out loud?
o: It reveals timing and delivery problems you cannot see silently

check.q: If you do not know the answer to a question, the best response is:
o: Say you do not know yet and explain how you would find out

check.q: When should you test your technology?
o: On the day, five minutes before

summary: Present your capstone, defend it under questions, reflect on your growth and plan what comes next.
goals: Deliver your capstone presentation clearly and confidently
Answer questions honestly and with evidence
Reflect on how you have grown across the year and set your next goals
idea: The Grand Summit is not a memory test. It is the moment your separate skills (communication, leadership, critical thinking, digital literacy, financial sense and community impact) are used together in front of real people. Judges will look at the quality of your project, the clarity of your delivery, how you handle questions and the growth visible across your portfolio.

The Summit is also a beginning. The habits you built, from reflection to feedback, from goal-setting to service, are what you take into school, university, work and life. The best way to honour the year is to decide what you will keep doing.
oneLine: Present, defend, reflect and keep growing: the Summit is a milestone, not the end.
steps: Present: start with your hook, tell the story of the problem and your solution, show your evidence and end with a clear call to action
Defend: listen to each question fully, pause, answer honestly with evidence and thank the questioner
Reflect: complete your Future Ready Passport and compare your Week 1 letter with who you are now
Next: write three goals for the next 12 months and name one person who will hold you accountable
scenarioSetup: On Summit day, Ada's slides freeze halfway through her presentation. A judge asks, 'What would you do differently if you had more funding?'
scenarioWrong: She panics, apologises repeatedly and gives a short answer. She then feels the year was wasted.
scenarioBetter: Present: she calmly switches to her backup and carries on using her notes
Defend: she pauses, then says, 'With more funding I would train 20 more volunteers and add a second venue; our data shows demand is higher than we can serve.'
Reflect: she reads her Week 1 letter and sees how much she has grown
Next: she writes goals for the next year and asks her mentor to meet quarterly.
mistakes: Mistake: apologising for small slips. Fix: Recover calmly and continue.
Mistake: ignoring the audience's questions. Fix: Listen fully and answer honestly.
Mistake: stopping when the programme ends. Fix: Keep your habits and goals alive.
lab: (10 min) Present your capstone to the group or panel
(10 min) Answer questions using Pause, Answer, Evidence
(10 min) Read your Week 1 letter and write what has changed
(5 min) Write three goals for the next year
reflect: What am I proudest of, beyond a trophy or a grade?
How have I changed since Week 1?
What will I keep doing every week?
takeaways: The Summit shows your skills working together
challenge: Complete your Future Ready Passport and final portfolio, write a thank-you note to someone who helped you this year, and set three goals for the next 12 months. Share your goals with your accountability partner.

check.q: What is the Grand Summit mainly about?
o: Using your skills together to present and defend a project

check.q: Your slides freeze during the presentation. What is the best response?
o: Stay calm, use your backup or notes and continue

check.q: What should you do after the programme ends?
o: Keep your habits, goals and accountability going
Wait for someone else to organise it
